title: Phase transitions and microphases in elastomers. I. Emergence of stable domains
authors: Manu Mannattil, Haim Diamant, David Andelman
abstract: Elasticity often plays a key role in regulating phase separation in physical systems. Recent experiments have shown that elastic effects can be used to control microphase separation in swollen elastomers. Here, microphase separation arises from a mismatch between the characteristic length scales of elastic and thermodynamic interactions. In this first part of a two-part paper, we show that microphase formation in elastomers can be explained using conventional theories of elasticity through a nonlocal thermodynamic-elastic coupling arising from volume conservation. Our theory reproduces the observed dependence of phase transition temperature and domain size on elastomer stiffness in isotropically swollen elastomers. In the companion paper, we investigate the effects of anisotropic swelling and inhomogeneous elastic moduli.
summary: This theoretical work models microphase separation in swollen elastomers by coupling thermodynamic fluctuations (Ginzburg-Landau) to elastic deformations. By deriving a nonlocal coupling from volume conservation, the authors show that elasticity dictates the morphology and transition temperature of these soft materials. This provides a generalized framework for understanding how mechanical constraints govern phase behavior.
main_problem: The paper investigates how elastic forces regulate phase separation, specifically microphase separation (EMPS), within swollen elastomer networks.
main_result: The theory successfully reproduces the experimentally observed scaling of domain size and transition temperature with elastomer stiffness by incorporating a nonlocal coupling arising from volume conservation.
method: The analysis uses continuum elasticity theory combined with Ginzburg-Landau free energy functionals, analyzed via Fourier space methods to study fluctuations around equilibrium states.
model_or_system: The system is an isotropically swollen crosslinked polymer network (elastomer). The model Hamiltonian combines a Ginzburg-Landau term for phase separation and a linear elastic energy term based on strain fields.
key_observables: Domain size, phase transition temperature ($T_m$), structure factor peak ($q_m$), and the dimensionless parameter $\gamma_0$.
important_parameters: Elastomer stiffness (Young's modulus $Y$), characteristic length scales ($\xi$, domain size), and material constants ($a, b, \kappa$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes small fluctuations near the critical point and initially restricts itself to isotropic swelling; anisotropic effects are reserved for a companion paper.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates scale separation in volume fraction ($\phi(x)$), showing that only variations beyond a characteristic length $h$ cause significant network deformations captured by coarse-graining.
paper_structure: The work is presented in two parts: Part I establishes the theory for isotropic swelling using nonlocal coupling derived from volume conservation. The companion paper (Part II) extends this analysis to include anisotropic swelling and inhomogeneous elastic moduli.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter elasticity, the mathematical framework involving coupled order parameters ($\psi$) and strain fields ($u$), analyzed via fluctuation theory in Fourier space, shares structural similarities with many-body field theories used in AMO physics for studying phase transitions in interacting quantum systems.
